R E P O R T
CHAPTER – I
Introductory
 
            The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the joint responsibility of the Ministries of Home Affairs (Services
and Establishment Wing) and Finance (Establishment Division) with Union Public Service Commission playing an important advisory role. The
Establishment Officer to the Government of India, functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the
Government of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified  Central direction.
 
2.         To plug this organisation loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha in its 93
rd Report (April 1966) observed that “the ever expanding
role of the government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil service calls for effective personnel control through a single agency”.
The Administrative Reforms Commission too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be placed directly under the Prime
Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel functions of the Government.
 
3.         The Union Government accepted this recommendation and as a consequence the ‘Department of Personnel’ was set up in August, 1970 and placed
within the Cabinet Secretariat. In February, 1973, the Department of Administrative Reforms, till then with the Ministry of Home Affairs, was amalgamated
with the Department of Personnel and the newly created department was christened, the ‘Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms’. In 1977, this
department was transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March, 1985 a full fledged ‘Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions’ was
created.
 
4.0       The Ministry is the coordinating agency of the Central Government in personnel matters specially issues concerning recruitment, training, career
development, staff welfare as well as the process of responsive people–oriented modern administration.  The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely: -
 
(i)                  Department of Personnel and Training.
(ii)             Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare.
(iii)
               Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
 
4.1       The Ministry has under its administrative control  four attached offices and four other offices, namely: -
 
            (i)            Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI);
(ii)
                Staff Selection Commission (SSC);
(iii)              Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM); and
(iv)              Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA).
 
 
The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are: -

5.         The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by two Ministers of State – one for the Department of Personnel and Training
and Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare and the other for the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances. All the three
Departments are functioning under the charge of the Secretary (Personnel) assisted by four Additional Secretaries and three Joint Secretaries and other
supporting officers and staff.
 
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGENCIES UNDER ITS ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL
 
6.0       The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided into two parts.  In its larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of
policy and the watch dog of the Government ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms, as laid down by it, are followed by all
Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of service conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues.  Towards this end,
guidelines are issued by it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors the implementation of these guidelines.  It also advises all
organisations of the Central Government  on issues of personnel management.  At a more immediate level, the Department has the direct responsibility of
being the cadre controlling authority for the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS).  The Department also operates the
Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers from  All India Services and Group ‘A’ Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the
level of Deputy Secretary, Director and Joint Secretary on the basis of tenure deputation.  The Department also deals with cases of appointment to posts of
Chairmen, Managing Directors, full-time functional Directors/Members of the Board of Management of various public sector undertakings/enterprises,
corporations, banks and financial institutions.  It also deals with the assignment of Indian experts to various developing countries.
 
Recruitment Agencies
6.1       The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of personnel for the Government are the Union Public Service Commission
(UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the Constitution and is responsible for conducting
examinations for appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment to the All India Services. There
is a mandatory provision for consulting the Commission on all matters relating to methods of  recruitment, principles to be followed in making promotions
and transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The SSC is responsible for making recruitment for Group ‘B’ non-gazetted posts of
Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
 
Training Institutions
6.2       Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the Department are the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of
Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The former   is   mainly   responsible  
for   providing   induction   training   to  recruits   to  the Indian Administrative Service and other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of
Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service training to members of the Central Secretariat Service.
 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India
6.3       All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the approval of the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
(ACC) are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary to the ACC.  These include board level appointments to Central Public Sector
Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments by
promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed through the Establishment Officer.
 
Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
 
6.4       The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board
level posts of Chief Executive and functional Directors and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Undertakings.
 
Administrative Vigilance
 
6.5       The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the maintenance of integrity of the public services and eradication of
corruption and coordinates the activities of various Ministries/Departments in that area.
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
6.6       Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and power in respect of all matters to which the
executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted with the supervision of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). The
Commission enjoys the same measure of independence and autonomy as the Union Public Service Commission.
 
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
 
6.7       The Central Bureau of Investigation is the premier investigating agency of the country to investigate complex and important cases particularly relating
to internal security, espionage, sabotage, narcotics, economic offences, cybercrimes and cases  registered under Preventing   Corruption  Act.
 
Joint Consultative Machinery
6.8       The Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) is three-tier machinery consisting of the National Council, the Departmental Council and the Regional/Office
Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the generality of employees or specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery.
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)

6.9       In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by Government decisions, the Government has set up the Central
Administrative Tribunal  (CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to service matters which were previously dealt with by Courts upto and
including the High Courts. 
 
Staff Welfare
 
6.10     The Department supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare
Coordination Committee in Central Government offices located outside Delhi, Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers; Benevolent Fund and
Departmental Canteens.  Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for three registered societies set up  for the welfare of the Government
employees and their families.  These societies are the Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra and Kendriya Bhandar. 
 
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
7.         The Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the Government of India for formulation of general policy on pension and
other retirement benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on retirement benefits.  The Department was set up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions and has been rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then.  Department has taken a number of steps over the
years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience and welfare of the pensioners.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
8.         The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well
as redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and grievances pertaining to  Central Government agencies in particular. The Department
disseminates information on important activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through Management
Publications and Documentation.  This Department also acts as the nodal agency in regard to Organisation and Methods activities and offers advice to the
Ministries/Departments. It also undertakes activities in the field of international co-operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.

CITIZEN’S CHARTER
 
14.0     The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances coordinates the efforts to formulate and operationalise citizen’s/user’s charter by
the Central Government Ministries/Departments and their PSUS/autonomous/statutory bodies in areas in which they provide services to the members of the
public. The Department also coordinates the efforts of formulating and operationalising citizen’s charter in various States/Uts.
 
14.1            Citizen’s charter has been modelled on pattern of charters prevalent in the United Kingdom but the Indian citizen’s charter has an additional
component of “expectations of the service providers from the users”. All other components, namely, (i) statement of the services provided (ii) standards of
service (time norms, locations, costs etc.) (iii) grievance redress mechanism (iv) mechanism of feedback are same under both the models.
 
14.2     The Committee wanted to know whether any specific time frame has been given to Ministries/Departments/Organisations and States/Uts for
formulation of citizen’s charters. The Ministry in its reply has stated that although no specific time frame has been given, yet the Department constantly
persue with these organization as a result of which the number of citizen’s charters formulated by Central Ministries/Departments/ Organisations have
increased from 61 to 68. Simarily, the number of charters formulated by 19 States/Union Territories have witness an increased trend from 200 to 313 during
the financial year 2000-2001.
 
14.3     To a question how the Government ensure involvement and participation of Members of Parliament, and State legislatures and opinion makers on the
evaluation/review of citizen’s charters to make them citizen-friendly, the Ministry has replied that Ministries/Departments/Organisations and States/UTs have
been advised to consult representatives of Consumer Groups, members of public, experts and representatives of the people at the time of  formulation of the
charter. It has been  further stated by the Ministry that the concerned organization is advised to set up a task force assisted by field agencies and
representatives of Consumer Groups to identify the nature of work and the client groups, nature of service provided and cost involved at the formulation time
of charter. Further the concerned organization are also advised by the Ministry to monitor/review/evaluate the citizen’s charter by internal as well as external
agencies such as consumer groups, NGOs and representatives of the charter.
 
14.4     From the replies of the Ministry elaborated in the previous paras, it seems that directions of the Ministry to ensure participation of Members of
Parliament, State Legislatures and opinion makers exist at the formulation stage and not at the evaluation stage of the citizen’s charter. The Committee
recommends that the feedback of the users must be assessed by the organizations providing services in the light of suggestion received from the
representatives of the people. The concerned organization must strive to find methods to ensure the participation of representatives of people in formulation as
well as evaluation of citizen’s charter.

Section 30 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985  provides that “ All proceedings   before a Tribunal shall be deemed to be judicial proceedings
within the meaning of sections 193, 219 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code.”
 
Rule 14(3) of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1987 provides that “The  Tribunal shall have the power to decline an
adjournment and also to limit the time for oral arguments.”
 
Rule 15 provides that when an applicant fails to appear on appointed day, the Tribunal may, in its discretion, either dismiss the application for default
or hear and decide it on  merit.  However, a protection has been given to the applicant to file an application within 30 days from the date of dismissal
to restore the same after satisfying the Tribunal for non-appearance.  Where a final decision has been given, the applicant can file an application for
review.
 
Rule 16 provides that when a respondent  fails to appear on appointed day, the Tribunal may, in its discretion, adjourn the hearing or hear and decide
the application ex-parte.  The respondents may apply within 30 days from the date of the  order to the Tribunal  for an order to set it aside and if such
respondent/s satisfy  the Tribunal   that the  notice was not duly served, or that he or they  were  prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing
when application came up for hearing, the Tribunal may make an order setting aside the ex-parte order  as against  him or them, upon such terms as it
thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the application.
 
Rule 19 further provides that the Tribunal may, if sufficient cause is shown  at any stage  of proceedings, grant  time to the parties or any of them, and 
adjourn the hearing of the application.  The Tribunal may make such  order as it thinks fit with respect to the costs occasioned by the adjournments.
 
As is evident from the above, the adjournments in the case/s is/are granted by the Tribunal in its judicial  capacity taking into account the
circumstances  of the case/s and  Government as a matter of policy does not issue directions related  to the judicial functioning of CAT as that may
construe interference in their judicial functioning.

19.11   The CAT’s functioning and the role played by it in arresting the reduction of pendency of service-related cases is not satisfactory.  Further, the
decision of the CAT can be  challenged   in the Division Bench of High  Court has put the deliverance  of inexpensive  and speedy  justice to the Government
employees in question.  The Committee feels that serious  thinking  on the functioning of the CAT has to be taken and in that context  takes into account   the
following suggestions of Law  Commission on the functioning  and structure  of the CAT in its 162nd Report.
 
(i)         The present practice of appointing retired or about to retire District Judges as  Judicial  members is not entirely satisfactory.  Since they did not
deal service matters earlier and there  is no time and in some of them,  inclination to learn  the service   jurisprudence.  Therefore, members of
Bar of the age  of 45  to 50 having experience  in service matters may be recruited for the initial period of ten years which required amendment 
of Section 8 of the A.T. Act, 1985.
(ii)        Administrative Member should not be appointed as Chairman/Vice-Chairman of CAT.
(iii)
              Constitution of a National Appellate  Administrative  Tribunal to entertain appeals against the orders  passed by the Administrative Tribunals
on the lines of the National Consumer Dispute  Redressal Commission created by the Consumers Protection Act, 1986.
(iv)              Selection  of Judicial Members from legal officers holding  atleast three years the post of Joint Secretary  and its equivalent through a process
of a high standard written examination.
(v)               Grouping of judgements pronounced by Courts for expeditious  disposal of cases by the CAT for which a Research Officer will be  appointed 
to assist  the Tribunal in increasing the expertise and efficiency of the CAT/SAT.
(vi)              Constitution of Benches of retired Members   of the   tribunal for disposal of pending cases.
(vii)            A proper litigation policy and machinery should be evolved by the Government/Public Sector Undertakings to curb litigation.
(viii)           Cost of raising frivolous defences to  be quantified by the Tribunal.
(ix)              Need to evolve  a mechanism for nipping in the bud the conflicting  interpretations  by the CAT/High Court.

(iii)               to advise the Government on the desired structure at the Board level, and for senior mangement personnel, for each PSE or group of PSEs;

Central Vigilance Commission Ordinances dated 25 August, 1998, 27 October, 1998 and 8 January 1999 lapsed after expiry of the prescribed period.  The

26.3     All State Governments are required to conduct a review of the career records and the character rolls of members of the service due to complete 30

Ministries/Departments should take stock of grievances received by them including their field agencies.  These grievances should be monitored by
Director (PG) and a quarterly report furnished to the Department of AR&PG.
Each Ministry/Department should prepare a consolidated directory of officers handling public/staff grievances in the Ministry/Department and
organizations under it.
Ministries/Departments should arrange publicizing their grievance redress mechanism through citizens Charters, broadcast of audio-visual capsules,
spots, websites etc.
Focus attention and analysis of public grievances to identify grievance prone areas and implement systemic changes to reduce grievances.
Brochure/Pamphlets prepared by various Ministries/Departments and their subordinate/attached/autonomous agencies may be kept at accessible contact
points including the railway stations,  bus stands etc.
Citizens’ level of satisfaction should be measured on a regular basis.
